title: One city
hook: if reason is shared and law is shared, we're fellow citizens of one city (Meditations 4.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Seneca, and his sailor without a harbor. Your line was on purpose.

Somebody once asked the philosopher Diogenes where he came from. The usual answer would have been a town: Sinope, on the Black Sea. Instead, the old story says, he answered: I am a citizen of the world. The Greek word was kosmopolites, where we get cosmopolitan. Five hundred years later, an emperor who ruled much of the known world built an argument under that one-liner, step by careful step. Today: one city.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU FROM?` → `A CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.` → `ONE CITY.`

segments.voice: Marcus begins the fourth entry of book four: if the power to think is common to all of us, then reason, which makes us reasoning creatures, is common too. You and the stranger at the bus stop have the same equipment. If reason is common, he goes on, then the reason that tells us what to do and not do is common. And if that's common, law is common. And if law is common, we are fellow citizens. We share in a kind of political life, and so the world is, in a way, a city. What other shared constitution, he asks, could the whole human race be said to share? He ends by asking where else our minds, our reason and our sense of law could come from, if not from this common source. Just as the earth, water, air and fire in his body come from somewhere, so does his mind. Notice what this does to a stranger. If you and the person cutting in line are citizens of one city, they're not an obstacle or an extra in your movie. They're a neighbor, maybe a badly behaved one, but a neighbor. Seneca, a few weeks back on this path, spoke of two cities, the local one and the great one. Marcus folds them closer: one city, and you were born in it. Elsewhere he says it plainly. A poet calls Athens dear city of Cecrops. Won't you call the world dear city of Zeus?
screen: `REASON IS SHARED.` · `SO LAW IS SHARED.` · `SO WE ARE FELLOW CITIZENS.` · `WHERE ELSE WOULD MIND COME FROM?` · then, large: `ONE CITY.`

segments.voice: Picture a stranger you'll probably pass today, a cashier, a driver, someone on the sidewalk, as clearly as you can. Say to yourself, gently: same reason, same law, same city. Notice whether anything shifts in you.
One city. Marcus reasons that shared reason means shared law, and shared law means we are all fellow citizens of one world-city. Today's word.
Your line: dear city of Zeus. The stranger in line is a neighbor too. That's day five hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often recall Meditations 4.4 with strangers, reminding themselves that shared reason makes everyone a fellow citizen of one world-city.

chat.says: How did Marcus get from shared reason to calling the world one city?
options: Shared reason means shared law, and shared law makes us all fellow citizens.
Rome ruled most of the known world, so he thought of it all as Rome's city.
Cities were full of strangers, so he thought the whole world felt like one.
chat.meaning: Marcus argues step by step: reason is common, so law is common, so we're fellow citizens, and the world is a kind of city.

Diogenes.meaning: Greek philosopher who called himself a citizen of the world

Sinope.meaning: Diogenes' hometown, on the Black Sea

kosmopolites.meaning: Greek for 'citizen of the world', source of 'cosmopolitan'

Cecrops.meaning: a mythic early king; the poet calls Athens his city

Zeus.meaning: the chief god of the ancient Greeks

notes: 4.4 paraphrased: if our intellectual part is common, reason is common; then the reason commanding what to do is common; then law is common; then we are fellow citizens, members of a political community, and the world is in a manner a state; from where else do we have intelligence, reason and law? As the earthy, watery, fiery parts of me come from some source, so does the intellectual part. Confirm.
4.23: 'The poet says, Dear city of Cecrops; and wilt not thou say, Dear city of Zeus?' (paraphrased, not quoted). Confirm.

Diogenes Laertius 6.63: asked where he came from, Diogenes said 'I am a citizen of the world' (kosmopolites). Sinope as his birthplace. 'Five hundred years later' is approximate (Diogenes 4th c. BCE; Marcus 2nd c. CE): confirm.
The reference to Seneca's 'two cities' refers to SPIRITUAL day 511 (carry 'two cities'); confirm.
4.4's elements (earthy, watery, airy/breath, hot and fiery) now listed as earth, water, air and fire; confirm.
